newsitem.title: JAPAN: New party says would rethink Japan-US military tie.
newsitem.headline: New party says would rethink Japan-US military tie.

text.p: The leader of Japan's newest political party, seeking to stand out in a crowded field of groups touting vague reform, said on Thursday he aimed to create conditions in which U.S. troops were no longer needed in the country.
"Japan as an independent country should not forever think that harbouring foreign troops is a matter of course," said Yukio Hatoyama, president of the Democratic Party, which was founded last week.

His remarks, made at a news conference, appeared to be an afterthought to his reply to a reporter's question about defence policy in which he said the party would maintain Japan's cautious interpretation of its pacifist Constitution, which bans overseas military action.

Hatoyama, who said foreign policy and defence issues were not likely to figure in October 20 parliamentary elections, offered no concrete plan or timetable for a U.S. troop withdrawal, saying only that Japan should contribute to stability in the Asian region.
He cited the uproar on the southern island of Okinawa after the rape last year of a local schoolgirl by U.S. servicemen as a sign Japan should begin to rethink its security ties.

Hatoyama's remarks will be closely scrutinised by the Democrats' potential coalition partners in an election in which neither of two conservative parties, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and Shinshinto (The New Frontier Party) are expected to capture a clear majority.
Both parties support the U.S. presence as essential to Japan's security.
Newspaper opinion polls have shown voters more willing to vote for the Democrats, whose policies are still on the drawing board, than for Shinshinto and other established parties.

However, analysts say the Democratic Party, and Hatoyama himself, could suffer from association with recent coalition governments. The party is made up of defectors from the Social Democratic Party and Sakigake, the two minority members of the coalition that enabled the LDP to regain power in June 1994 after a brief stint in opposition.
Analysts say the Democratic Party's popularity stems from voter despair at a confusing and unappetising political menu, rather than any taste for the party itself.
"Their policy platform is a mishmash," said conservative critic Masaya Ito, who is close to the LDP.

Hatoyama said his party had not ruled out joining forces with either conservative party, but would "make no easy compromises" if invited to join government after polls, referring to economic and administrative reform.

He said the party would not repeat the mistake of the short-lived coalition governments -- of which he was a member -- that briefly shook up Japan's staid politics in 1993-94 before succumbing to fatigue and allowing unelected bureaucrats to take control.

"The four coalition governments since that time have, to the public, appeared to be little more than a political game being played out in Nagata-cho," Hatoyama said, referring to Tokyo's equivalent of Capital Hill.

Expectations that politicians would assert control over Japan's powerful bureaucracy, raised by those governments "have been supplanted by an even deeper mistrust of politics and an even darker perception of the future," he said.
However, Hatoyama's own critics are sceptical about his ability to reverse this trend, not least because he has been part of the governments he criticised.
"Hatoyama has not achieved any policy goals in the past," said political analyst Minoru Morita. "All he has done is to sit in the ruling camp."
